Content:
Hungarian here (an actual one, not just a descendant as all other commenters seem to be for some reason, dont mean any offense its just interesting).
Paprika really is our staple spice (sweet, smoked, spicy, all of them), and is used in most of our dishes.
Just as a prerequisite I would like to say what in english you would call Gulyás is actually two very separate hungarian staple dishes.
One is the Gulyás soup/stew (the one you made) and the ither is actually called Pörkölt in hungarian (literally meaning burned), which is more of a ragu with cubed meat, rather than a soup consistency.
While the history side you shared is kind of flawed (Only cattle herdsmen were called Gulyás (Gulya being used to refer to a group of cattle), also them being called Gulyás was only prevalent in on part of the country (Alföld, which is a big agricultural flat land with a huge influence on national culture, hence the Gulyás being prevalent) and was mostly prevalent after the end of the 18th/beginning of the 19th century, so hungarians in the 9th century and for a long time after that would not call herdsmen Gulyás.
Love the video tho

Content: Actually, the story of goulash goes much further than that. When we were at the Balaton in the late 80s, we were introduced to Hungarian goulash, wich was closer to a pork-and-potato soup than what we knew as Gulasch in Germany, and while there was undoubtedly paprika in there, there was much less than in our version. Later I learned that in many of the countries of eastern Europe around Hungary, the word "goulash" is used in the meaning of simply "stew".

Author: @markotisovic8233
Content:
We in Slovenia do it in simplest of ways and much thicker. 
Beef meet from the side (the sinewy part) or deer (for hunters gulash), onions in approx. 1:1 ratio in weight, red "sweet" powdered paprika (my favorite is from Horgosh Serbia), garlic, bay leaves and that is basicly more or less it (some add carrots  and/or a bit of hot pepers).
If you use beef side you basicly have to cook it for minimum 3-4 hours on small fire so sinews melt in your mouth and not be chewy and onions basicly desolves giving it thick texture (if you have to add flover you seriously screwed up as per my grandma).

Paprikash is basicly the same with other meats (chicken, rabbit, pork...)

As side dish just bread or boiled potato or polenta or macaroni
